new_statements.quote: The stresses employed metrically were those used in the normal pronunciation of Quenya. The main (high-toned) stress was originally on the first syllable of all words, but in words of 3 or more syllables it had been moved forward to fall on the penultimate syllable [second-to-last], if that were long; if it were short, it fell on the antepenult [third-to-last] irrespective of length, (as in éleni) (RGEO/60). [...] In The Lord of the Rings Appendix E Tolkien said "In words of two syllables it falls in practically all cases on the first syllable (LotR/1116)"

new_statements.rule_in_words: Latin-type quantity-sensitive stress with a three-syllable window: in words of three or more syllables the main stress falls on the penult if it is heavy (long vowel, diphthong ai/au/eu/oi/ui/iu, or a vowel followed by two or more consonants, including ny/ly/ry/ty/qu), otherwise on the antepenult regardless of its own weight; disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; the final syllable is never stressed in polysyllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes (RGEO/60-61, PE19/60-61 as quoted in Eldamo): the initial syllable usually keeps a secondary stress, in long words and compounds often equal in force to the main stress though lower in tone (óromárdi, fálmalínnar); it is weaker when it immediately precedes the main stress and is lost if that syllable is short (avā́nier); in words ending in two short syllables the final syllable carries a light secondary stress usable metrically (ūnōtime, tellumar). Tolkien marks primary stress with acute and secondary with grave; main stress carries the highest pitch except that a strong initial secondary in compounds may be higher in pitch (PE19/61).
new_statements.exceptions: 'practically all' disyllables initial: the suffixed imperative avá 'don't!' is stressed on the last syllable (WJ/371; also Ardalambion). Stressed monosyllabic pronouns in phrases lengthen their vowel (ní, tyé, sé; VT49/51). Prosodic lengthening of a light penult before case endings (ciryalíva) keeps the pattern regular. Early 'Qenya' (1910s, PE12/26-27) allowed stress four syllables from the end in quadrisyllables with two internal vowels in hiatus (Áreanòr) -- superseded in Late Quenya.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress, applying to inflected and uninflected forms alike; phrase-level notes: unstressed clitic-like monosyllables (ve, i, an) vs stressed content monosyllables (sī, man, nin) in verse (RGEO/68). Stress described as non-phonemic/predictable. The RGEO passage is written within Tolkien's fictional history ('originally.. had been moved forward').
new_statements.identity_note: Quenya is a constructed language (J.R.R. Tolkien); Glottolog quen1234 carries no descriptive bibliography. The rule quoted is for 'Late Quenya' (Tolkien's post-1950 conception, the LotR-era language, Exilic/Noldorin Quenya as spoken in Middle-earth); Eldamo notes that Tolkien's 1910s 'Qenya' (PE12) had a slightly different system (stress could reach the fourth syllable from the end in a hiatus case). Wikipedia notes a Parmaquesta vs colloquial Tarquesta difference only in whether hy/hw close a syllable. All quotations are Tolkien's own words as reproduced verbatim with page locators in Eldamo (a fan-scholarship lexicon by Paul Strack) and Fauskanger's Ardalambion course; the print primaries (LotR App. E p. 1116; RGEO pp. 60-61; PE19 pp. 59-61) were not themselves opened.

sources.note: Stress predictable and non-phonemic, weight-sensitive: disyllables on the first syllable; 3+ syllables on the penult if heavy (long vowel, diphthong, or closed syllable, incl. before ll, ld, mm, ss, ny, ry), else on the antepenult; same as Latin; a secondary accent exists; hy and hw close a syllable in Parmaquesta but not colloquially in Tarquesta.

sources.note: Follows LotR Appendix E: quotes Tolkien 'in words of two syllables [the accent] falls in practically all cases on the first syllable'; in words of 3+ syllables the penult is stressed if it has a long vowel, a diphthong (ai, au, eu, oi, ui, iu) or a short vowel followed by more than one consonant (ny, ly, ry, ty, qu count as clusters), otherwise stress moves to the antepenult; quotes Tolkien that words of that shape 'are favoured in the Eldarin languages, especially Quenya'; only known exception ava 'don't!' stressed finally; examples VESTale, ElenTARi, ElENDil, ErESSea, SilmaRILLion.

sources.note: Reproduces Tolkien's rule verbatim with locators: main stress on the penult if heavy (long vowel, diphthong, or vowel + 2+ consonants), otherwise on the antepenult; disyllables stressed on the first syllable; secondary stress on the initial syllable (weak if immediately before the main stress and light), light secondary stress on the final of words ending in two light syllables; exception: suffixed imperative ava 'don't' stressed on the last syllable (WJ/371); stressed monosyllables in phrases lengthen their vowel; main stress carries the highest pitch (PE19/61).
